1.0.oldText: Mr. Utterson the lawyer was a man of rough features that never lit up with a smile—cold, sparing, and awkward in conversation; reserved in feeling; lean, long, dusty, dreary, and yet somehow lovable. At friendly gatherings, when the wine suited his taste, something deeply human shone from his eye—something that never made it into his speech, but spoke not only in the silent signs on his post-dinner face, but louder and more often in the actions of his life. He was strict with himself: he drank gin alone, to discipline his taste for fine wines; and though he enjoyed the theatre, he had not crossed the door of one in twenty years. But he extended a settled tolerance to others—sometimes wondering, almost with envy, at the wild energy that drove their misdeeds; and in any extremity he was inclined to help rather than condemn. “I lean towards Cain’s heresy,” he used to say in his quaint way (Cain being the man in Genesis who asked, “Am I my brother’s keeper?”): “I let my brother go to the devil in his own way.” In this role it was often his lot to be the last respectable acquaintance and the last good influence in the lives of men who were going down. And towards such men, as long as they came to his rooms, he never showed the slightest change in his manner.

1.1.oldText: This was no doubt easy for Mr. Utterson, since he was undemonstrative at the best of times, and even his friendships seemed founded on a similar broad good-nature. It is the mark of a modest man to accept his circle of friends ready-made from the hands of chance; and that was the lawyer’s way. His friends were either blood relations or men he had known the longest; his affections, like ivy, were the growth of time, and implied nothing special about their object. Hence, no doubt, the bond between him and Mr. Richard Enfield, his distant kinsman, the well-known man about town. What these two could see in each other, or what subject they could find in common, was a puzzle to many. People who met them on their Sunday walks reported that they said nothing, looked unusually dull, and would greet the appearance of a friend with obvious relief. Still, the two men placed the highest value on these outings, counted them the chief jewel of each week, and not only put aside chances for pleasure but even resisted business calls so they could enjoy them uninterrupted.

1.2.oldText: On one of these rambles, their walk happened to lead them down a side street in a busy quarter of London. The street was small and what people called quiet, but on weekdays it did a thriving trade. The residents all seemed to be doing well, and all were eager to do better still, spending the surplus of their earnings on display; so the shop fronts along that thoroughfare stood with an inviting air, like rows of smiling saleswomen. Even on Sunday, when the street veiled its more showy charms and lay comparatively empty of traffic, it shone out against its grimy neighbourhood like a fire in a forest; and with its freshly painted shutters, well-polished brasswork, and overall cleanliness and cheerfulness, it instantly caught and pleased the eye of any passerby.

1.3.oldText: Two doors from one corner, on the left going east, the line of buildings was broken by the entrance of a courtyard; and at that very point a sinister block of building thrust its gable forward onto the street. It was two storeys high, showed no window—nothing but a door on the lower floor and a blind, discoloured wall above—and bore in every feature the marks of long and squalid neglect. The door, which had neither bell nor knocker, was blistered and stained. Tramps slouched into the recess and struck matches on the panels; children kept shop on the steps; schoolboys had tried their knives on the mouldings; and for nearly a generation no one had appeared to drive away these random visitors or repair the damage they did.

1.4.oldText: Mr. Enfield and the lawyer were on the other side of the side street; but as they came abreast of the entry, Enfield lifted his cane and pointed.

1.5.oldText: “Did you ever notice that door?” he asked; and when his companion said yes, he added, “In my mind it’s connected with a very strange story.”

1.6.oldText: “Really?” said Mr. Utterson, with a slight change in his voice. “And what was that?”

1.7.oldText: “Well, it was like this,” Mr. Enfield said. “I was walking home from a place at the end of the world, about three o’clock on a black winter morning, and my route took me through a part of town where there was literally nothing to be seen but lamps. Street after street with everyone asleep—street after street lit up as if for a procession and as empty as a church—until at last I reached that state of mind where a man listens and listens and starts to long for the sight of a policeman. All at once I saw two figures: one a small man stumping along eastward at a brisk pace, and the other a girl of maybe eight or ten running as fast as she could down a cross street. Well, sir, the two ran into each other naturally enough at the corner; and then came the horrible part of the thing. The man trampled calmly right over the child’s body and left her screaming on the ground. It sounds like nothing to hear, but it was hellish to see. It wasn’t like a man; it was like some damned juggernaut. I shouted, took off after him, grabbed my gentleman, and brought him back to where a group had already gathered around the screaming child. He was perfectly cool and made no resistance, but he gave me one look—so ugly that it brought the sweat out on me as if I’d been running. The people who had come out were the girl’s own family; and pretty soon the doctor they had sent for arrived. Well, the child wasn’t much the worse for it—more frightened than anything, according to the doctor; and you’d think that would be the end of it. But there was one odd thing. I had taken a loathing to my gentleman the moment I saw him. So had the child’s family, naturally enough. But what struck me was the doctor’s case. He was the usual cut-and-dry apothecary—the ordinary kind of doctor of the day—of no particular age or colour, with a strong Edinburgh accent, and about as emotional as a bagpipe. Well, sir, he was like the rest of us: every time he looked at my prisoner, I saw that doctor turn sick and white with the desire to kill him. I knew what was in his mind, just as he knew what was in mine; and since killing was out of the question, we did the next best thing. We told the man we could and would make such a scandal out of this that his name would stink from one end of London to the other. If he had any friends or any credit, we said, we’d see that he lost them. And the whole time, as we were laying it on red-hot, we were keeping the women off him as best we could, because they were as wild as harpies. I never saw a circle of such hateful faces; and there was the man in the middle, with a kind of black sneering coolness—frightened too, I could see—but carrying it off, sir, really like Satan. ‘If you choose to make capital out of this accident,’ said he, ‘I am naturally helpless. No gentleman likes to make a scene,’ he said. ‘Name your figure.’ Well, we screwed him up to a hundred pounds for the child’s family; he clearly would have liked to hold out, but there was something about the lot of us that meant trouble, and at last he gave in. The next thing was to get the money; and where do you think he led us, but to that place with the door?—whipped out a key, went in, and presently came back with about ten pounds in gold and a cheque for the rest on Coutts’s bank, drawn payable to bearer and signed with a name I can’t mention—though it’s one of the points of my story—but a name at least very well known and often in print. The amount was steep; but the signature was good for more than that, if only it was genuine. I took the liberty of pointing out to my gentleman that the whole business looked fishy, and that a man does not, in real life, walk into a cellar door at four in the morning and come out with another man’s cheque for nearly a hundred pounds. But he was quite easy and sneering. ‘Set your mind at rest,’ he said, ‘I will stay with you till the banks open and cash the cheque myself.’ So we all set off—the doctor, the child’s father, our friend, and me—and spent the rest of the night in my rooms; and the next morning, after breakfast, we went in a body to the bank. I handed in the cheque myself, and said I had every reason to believe it was a forgery. Not a bit of it. The cheque was genuine.”

1.9.oldText: “I see you feel as I do,” said Mr. Enfield. “Yes, it’s a bad story. Because my man was a fellow nobody could have to do with, a really damnable man; and the person who drew the cheque is the very picture of propriety, well-known too, and (what makes it worse) one of those people who do what they call good. Blackmail, I suppose: an honest man paying through the nose for some of the wild capers of his youth. ‘Black Mail House’ is what I call the place with the door, as a result. Though even that, you know, is far from explaining everything,” he added, and with the words fell into a thoughtful silence.

1.10.oldText: From this he was recalled when Mr. Utterson asked rather suddenly, “And you don’t know whether the man who drew the cheque lives there?”

1.11.oldText: “A likely place, isn’t it?” returned Mr. Enfield. “But I happen to have noticed his address; he lives in some square or other.”

1.12.oldText: “And you never asked about the—place with the door?” said Mr. Utterson.

1.13.oldText: “No, sir; I had a kind of delicacy about it,” was the reply. “I feel very strongly about asking questions; it has too much of the day-of-judgment about it. You start a question, and it’s like starting a stone. You sit quietly on the top of a hill, and away the stone goes, starting others; and presently some bland old fellow (the last one you would have thought of) is knocked on the head in his own back garden and the family has to change their name. No, sir; I have a rule of mine: the more it looks like Queer Street—like trouble, or something shady—the less I ask.”

1.15.oldText: “But I’ve studied the place for myself,” Mr. Enfield went on. “It scarcely seems a house. There is no other door, and nobody goes in or out of that one but, once in a great while, the gentleman of my adventure. There are three windows looking onto the court on the first floor; none below; the windows are always shut, but they’re clean. And then there’s a chimney that’s generally smoking; so somebody must live there. And yet it’s not certain even then, because the buildings around the court are packed so tightly together that it’s hard to say where one ends and another begins.”

1.16.oldText: The pair walked on again for a while in silence; and then, “Enfield,” said Mr. Utterson, “that’s a good rule of yours.”

1.17.oldText: “Yes, I think it is,” returned Enfield.

1.18.oldText: “But for all that,” the lawyer continued, “there’s one point I want to ask. I want to ask the name of that man who walked over the child.”

1.19.oldText: “Well,” said Mr. Enfield, “I can’t see what harm it would do. It was a man by the name of Hyde.”

1.20.oldText: “Hm,” said Mr. Utterson. “What sort of man is he to look at?”

1.21.oldText: “He’s not easy to describe. There is something wrong with his appearance; something displeasing, something downright detestable. I never saw a man I disliked so much, and yet I scarcely know why. He must be deformed somewhere; he gives a strong feeling of deformity, although I couldn’t point to exactly what. He’s an extraordinary-looking man, and yet I really can’t name anything out of the way about him. No, sir; I can make nothing of it; I can’t describe him. And it isn’t for lack of memory, because I tell you I can see him this very moment.”

1.22.oldText: Mr. Utterson again walked some way in silence, obviously under the weight of consideration. “You’re sure he used a key?” he asked at last.

1.23.oldText: “My dear sir…” began Enfield, surprised out of himself.

1.24.oldText: “Yes, I know,” said Utterson. “I know it must seem strange. The fact is, if I don’t ask you the name of the other party, it’s because I already know it. You see, Richard, your tale has hit home. If you’ve been inexact on any point, you had better correct it.”

1.25.oldText: “I think you might have warned me,” returned the other with a touch of sullenness. “But I have been pedantically exact, as you call it. The fellow had a key; and what’s more, he still has it. I saw him use it not a week ago.”

1.26.oldText: Mr. Utterson sighed deeply but didn’t say a word; and presently the young man went on. “Here’s another lesson to say nothing,” he said. “I’m ashamed of my long tongue. Let’s make a bargain never to refer to this again.”

1.27.oldText: “With all my heart,” said the lawyer. “I shake hands on that, Richard.”

2.0.oldText: That evening Mr. Utterson came home to his bachelor house in a sombre mood and sat down to dinner with no appetite. It was his Sunday custom, once dinner was over, to sit close by the fire with some dry theological volume on his reading desk until the clock of the neighbouring church struck twelve, when he would go soberly and gratefully to bed. On this night, however, as soon as the tablecloth was cleared, he took up a candle and went into his business room. There he opened his safe, took from the most private part of it a document marked on the envelope as Dr. Jekyll’s Will, and sat down with a clouded brow to study its contents. The will was holographic—written entirely in Jekyll’s own hand—because Mr. Utterson—though he had taken charge of it once it was made—had refused to give the slightest help in making it. It provided that if Henry Jekyll, M.D., D.C.L., L.L.D., F.R.S., etc., should die, everything he owned would pass to his “friend and benefactor Edward Hyde.” But it went further: in case of Dr. Jekyll’s “disappearance or unexplained absence for any period exceeding three calendar months,” Edward Hyde was to step straight into his place without further delay, free of any burden beyond a few small payments to the doctor’s household. This document had long been an eyesore to the lawyer. It offended him both as a lawyer and as a man who loved the sane and conventional sides of life, and who found anything fanciful immodest. Until now it had been his ignorance of Mr. Hyde that swelled his indignation; now, by a sudden turn, it was his knowledge. It was already bad enough when the name was only a name about which he could learn nothing more. It was worse when it began to be clothed in detestable attributes; and out of the shifting, insubstantial mists that had so long baffled him, there leapt up the sudden, definite image of a fiend.

2.1.oldText: “I thought it was madness,” he said, as he put the offensive paper back in the safe, “and now I begin to fear it’s disgrace.”

2.2.oldText: With that he blew out his candle, put on a heavy overcoat, and set out towards Cavendish Square, that citadel of medicine, where his friend the great Dr. Lanyon had his house and received his many patients. “If anyone knows, it will be Lanyon,” he had thought.

2.3.oldText: The solemn butler knew him and welcomed him in. He was subjected to no waiting at all, but shown straight from the door to the dining-room, where Dr. Lanyon sat alone over his wine. This was a hearty, healthy, dapper, red-faced gentleman, with a shock of prematurely white hair and a boisterous, decided manner. At the sight of Mr. Utterson he sprang up from his chair and welcomed him with both hands. The friendliness, as was the man’s way, was somewhat theatrical to the eye, but it rested on genuine feeling. The two were old friends, old mates at school and college, both thoroughly self-respecting and respectful of each other, and—what doesn’t always follow—men who genuinely enjoyed each other’s company.

2.4.oldText: After a little rambling small talk, the lawyer led up to the subject that was so unpleasantly on his mind.

2.5.oldText: “I suppose, Lanyon,” he said, “you and I must be the two oldest friends Henry Jekyll has?”

2.6.oldText: “I wish the friends were younger,” chuckled Dr. Lanyon. “But I suppose we are. And what of that? I see little of him now.”

2.7.oldText: “Really?” said Utterson. “I thought you had a bond of common interest.”

2.8.oldText: “We had,” was the reply. “But it’s more than ten years since Henry Jekyll became too fanciful for me. He started to go wrong—wrong in mind; and though of course I keep up an interest in him for old times’ sake, as they say, I see, and have seen, devilishly little of the man. Such unscientific balderdash,” added the doctor, suddenly flushing purple, “would have estranged Damon and Pythias—the most devoted friends in legend.”

2.9.oldText: This little burst of temper was something of a relief to Mr. Utterson. “They’ve only differed on some point of science,” he thought; and being a man of no scientific passions himself (except in the matter of conveyancing—the legal work of transferring property), he even added, “It’s nothing worse than that!” He gave his friend a few seconds to recover, and then approached the question he had come to ask. “Did you ever come across a protégé of his—one Hyde?” he asked.

2.10.oldText: “Hyde?” Lanyon repeated. “No. Never heard of him. Since my time.”

2.11.oldText: That was the sum of the information the lawyer carried back with him to the great, dark bed on which he tossed and turned until the small hours of the morning began to grow large. It was a night of little ease for his toiling mind, toiling in sheer darkness and besieged by questions.

2.12.oldText: Six o’clock struck on the bells of the church so conveniently near to Mr. Utterson’s house, and still he was digging at the problem. So far it had touched him only intellectually; but now his imagination was engaged as well, or rather enslaved. As he lay tossing in the heavy darkness of the night and the curtained room, Mr. Enfield’s tale ran past his mind in a scroll of lighted pictures. He would be aware of the great field of lamps of a city at night; then of the figure of a man walking quickly; then of a child running from the doctor’s; and then these met, and that human juggernaut trampled the child and walked on, indifferent to her screams. Or else he would see a room in a wealthy house, where his friend lay asleep, dreaming and smiling at his dreams; and then the door of that room would open, the curtains of the bed would be pulled apart, the sleeper called back, and there at his side would stand a figure to whom power had been given—and at that dead hour he would have to rise and do its bidding. The figure in these two phases haunted the lawyer all night; and if he ever dozed off, it was only to see it glide more stealthily through sleeping houses, or move ever more swiftly, even dizzyingly, through wider labyrinths of lamp-lit city, and at every street corner crush a child and leave her screaming. And still the figure had no face by which he might know it; even in his dreams it had no face, or one that baffled him and melted before his eyes. And so there sprang up and grew quickly in the lawyer’s mind a singularly strong, almost excessive curiosity to see the features of the real Mr. Hyde. If he could only set eyes on him once, he thought, the mystery would lighten and perhaps roll right away, as mysteries tend to do when well examined. He might see a reason for his friend’s strange preference for Hyde—or his bondage to him, call it which you please—and even for the startling clauses of the will. At the very least it would be a face worth seeing: the face of a man without bowels of mercy—a man without pity—a face that had only to show itself to raise, in the mind of the unimpressionable Enfield, a spirit of enduring hatred.

2.13.oldText: From that time on, Mr. Utterson began to haunt the door in the side street of shops. In the morning before office hours, at noon when business was busy and time was short, at night under the face of the foggy city moon, by every light and at every hour of solitude or crowd, the lawyer was to be found at his chosen post.

2.14.oldText: “If he is Mr. Hyde,” he had thought, “I shall be Mr. Seek.”

2.15.oldText: And at last his patience was rewarded. It was a fine dry night; frost in the air; the streets as clean as a ballroom floor; the lamps, unshaken by any wind, drawing a regular pattern of light and shadow. By ten o’clock, when the shops were closed, the side street was very lonely and, in spite of the low growl of London all around, very silent. Small sounds carried far; the domestic sounds out of the houses were clearly audible on either side of the road; and the murmur of any approaching passerby preceded him for a long time. Mr. Utterson had been at his post for some minutes when he became aware of an odd light footstep drawing near. In the course of his nightly patrols he had long grown used to the quaint effect with which the footfalls of a single person, while he is still a great way off, suddenly stand out distinctly from the vast hum and clatter of the city. Yet his attention had never before been so sharply and decisively arrested; and it was with a strong, superstitious foresight of success that he withdrew into the entry of the court.

2.16.oldText: The steps drew swiftly nearer, and swelled suddenly louder as they turned the end of the street. The lawyer, looking out from the entry, could soon see what kind of man he had to deal with. He was small and very plainly dressed, and the look of him, even at that distance, somehow went strongly against the watcher’s feelings. But he made straight for the door, crossing the road to save time; and as he came, he drew a key from his pocket like someone approaching home.

2.17.oldText: Mr. Utterson stepped out and touched him on the shoulder as he passed. “Mr. Hyde, I think?”

2.18.oldText: Mr. Hyde shrank back with a hissing intake of breath. But his fear was only momentary; and though he did not look the lawyer in the face, he answered coolly enough: “That is my name. What do you want?”

2.19.oldText: “I see you’re going in,” returned the lawyer. “I am an old friend of Dr. Jekyll’s—Mr. Utterson of Gaunt Street—you must have heard of my name; and meeting you so conveniently, I thought you might let me in.”

2.20.oldText: “You won’t find Dr. Jekyll; he’s away from home,” replied Mr. Hyde, blowing in the key. And then suddenly, but still without looking up, “How did you know me?” he asked.

2.21.oldText: “For your part,” said Mr. Utterson, “will you do me a favour?”

2.22.oldText: “With pleasure,” replied the other. “What shall it be?”

2.24.oldText: Mr. Hyde appeared to hesitate, and then, as if upon some sudden thought, turned to face him with an air of defiance; and the pair stared at each other quite fixedly for a few seconds. “Now I shall know you again,” said Mr. Utterson. “It may be useful.”

2.25.oldText: “Yes,” returned Mr. Hyde, “it’s just as well we’ve met; and, à propos, you should have my address.” And he gave a number on a street in Soho.

2.26.oldText: “Good God!” thought Mr. Utterson, “can he too have been thinking of the will?” But he kept his feelings to himself and only grunted in acknowledgment of the address.

2.30.oldText: “We have common friends,” said Mr. Utterson.

2.31.oldText: “Common friends,” echoed Mr. Hyde, a little hoarsely. “Who are they?”

2.33.oldText: “He never told you,” cried Mr. Hyde, with a flush of anger. “I didn’t think you would have lied.”

2.34.oldText: “Come,” said Mr. Utterson, “that is not fitting language.”

2.35.oldText: The other snarled aloud into a savage laugh; and the next moment, with extraordinary quickness, he had unlocked the door and disappeared into the house.

2.36.oldText: The lawyer stood awhile after Mr. Hyde had left him, the picture of unease. Then he began slowly to climb the street, pausing every step or two and putting his hand to his brow like a man in mental confusion. The problem he was debating as he walked was one of a kind that is rarely solved. Mr. Hyde was pale and dwarfish; he gave an impression of deformity without any nameable malformation; he had a displeasing smile; he had carried himself towards the lawyer with a sort of murderous mixture of timidity and boldness; and he spoke in a husky, whispering, somewhat broken voice. All these were points against him, but not all of them together could explain the hitherto unknown disgust, loathing, and fear with which Mr. Utterson regarded him. “There must be something else,” said the perplexed gentleman. “There is something more, if only I could find a name for it. God bless me, the man hardly seems human! Something troglodytic—like a cave-dweller—shall we say? Or can it be the old story of Dr. Fell—disliking a man without being able to say why? Or is it the mere radiance of a foul soul that shines through and transforms its clay shell? The last, I think; because, O my poor old Harry Jekyll, if ever I read Satan’s signature on a face, it is on the face of your new friend.”

2.37.oldText: Round the corner from the side street there was a square of old, handsome houses, now mostly fallen from their former dignity and let out in flats and chambers to all sorts of men: map-engravers, architects, shady lawyers, and agents of obscure enterprises. One house, however, second from the corner, was still occupied as a single residence; and at the door of this house, which wore a great air of wealth and comfort—though it was now plunged in darkness except for the fanlight—Mr. Utterson stopped and knocked. A well-dressed, elderly servant opened the door.

2.39.oldText: “I will see, Mr. Utterson,” said Poole, admitting the visitor as he spoke into a large, low-ceilinged, comfortable hall paved with flagstones, warmed (in the style of a country house) by a bright open fire, and furnished with costly oak cabinets. “Will you wait here by the fire, sir? Or shall I bring you a light in the dining-room?”

2.40.oldText: “Here, thank you,” said the lawyer, and he drew near and leaned on the tall fender. This hall, where he was now left alone, was a pet favourite of his friend the doctor’s; and Utterson himself often spoke of it as the pleasantest room in London. But tonight there was a shudder in his blood; the face of Hyde sat heavy on his memory; he felt (what was rare with him) a nausea and distaste for life; and in the gloom of his spirits he seemed to read a threat in the flicker of the firelight on the polished cabinets and in the uneasy starting of the shadow on the ceiling. He was ashamed of his relief when Poole presently came back to say that Dr. Jekyll was out.

2.41.oldText: “I saw Mr. Hyde go in by the old dissecting-room door, Poole,” he said. “Is that right, when Dr. Jekyll is away from home?”

2.42.oldText: “Quite right, Mr. Utterson, sir,” replied the servant. “Mr. Hyde has a key.”

2.43.oldText: “Your master seems to place a great deal of trust in that young man, Poole,” the other resumed thoughtfully.

2.44.oldText: “Yes, sir, he does indeed,” said Poole. “We all have orders to obey him.”

2.45.oldText: “I don’t think I ever met Mr. Hyde?” asked Utterson.

2.46.oldText: “Oh, dear no, sir. He never dines here,” replied the butler. “Indeed we see very little of him on this side of the house; he mostly comes and goes by the laboratory.”

2.49.oldText: And the lawyer set out homeward with a very heavy heart. “Poor Harry Jekyll,” he thought, “I fear he is in deep water! He was wild when he was young; a long while ago, to be sure; but in the law of God there is no statute of limitations. Ah, that must be it—the ghost of some old sin, the cancer of some hidden disgrace: punishment coming, pede claudo—on limping foot—years after memory has forgotten and self-love forgiven the fault.” And the lawyer, frightened by the thought, brooded for a while on his own past, groping in every corner of memory in case some jack-in-the-box of an old wrongdoing might leap to light there. His past was fairly blameless; few men could read the records of their life with less apprehension; and yet he was humbled to the dust by the many bad things he had done, and lifted up again into a sober and fearful gratitude by the many he had come so close to doing yet had avoided. And then, returning to his earlier subject, he conceived a spark of hope. “This Master Hyde, if one studied him,” he thought, “must have secrets of his own—black secrets, by the look of him; secrets compared with which poor Jekyll’s worst would be like sunshine. Things cannot continue as they are. It turns me cold to think of this creature stealing like a thief to Harry’s bedside; poor Harry, what a waking! And the danger of it; because if this Hyde suspects that the will exists, he may grow impatient to inherit. Ah, I must put my shoulder to the wheel—if Jekyll will only let me,” he added, “if Jekyll will only let me.” For once again he saw before his mind’s eye, as clear as glass, the strange clauses of the will.

5.0.oldText: It was late in the afternoon when Mr. Utterson made his way to Dr. Jekyll’s door, where Poole let him in at once and led him down through the kitchen quarters and across a yard that had once been a garden, to the building known indifferently as the laboratory or the dissecting rooms. The doctor had bought the house from the heirs of a celebrated surgeon, and since his own interests ran more to chemistry than to anatomy, he had changed the use of the block at the bottom of the garden. This was the first time the lawyer had been received in that part of his friend’s quarters, and he eyed the dingy, windowless building with curiosity, looking around with an uneasy sense of strangeness as he crossed the operating theatre—once crowded with eager students and now standing gaunt and silent, its tables loaded with chemical apparatus, its floor littered with crates and packing straw, the light falling dimly through the grimy skylight. At the far end, a flight of stairs led up to a door covered in red baize; and through this Mr. Utterson was finally shown into the doctor’s private study. It was a large room lined with glass cabinets, furnished among other things with a full-length mirror and a desk, and looking out over the courtyard through three dusty, iron-barred windows. A fire burned in the grate; a lamp stood lit on the mantel, for even indoors the fog had begun to settle thick; and there, close by the warmth, sat Dr. Jekyll, looking deathly ill. He did not rise to greet his visitor, but held out a cold hand and welcomed him in a changed voice.

5.1.oldText: “And now,” said Mr. Utterson, as soon as Poole had left them, “you’ve heard the news?”

5.2.oldText: The doctor shuddered. “They were shouting it in the square,” he said. “I heard them from my dining room.”

5.3.oldText: “One word,” said the lawyer. “Carew was my client, but so are you, and I want to know what I’m doing. You haven’t been mad enough to hide this fellow?”

5.4.oldText: “Utterson, I swear to God,” cried the doctor, “I swear to God I will never set eyes on him again. I give you my word of honour that I’m done with him in this world. It’s all over. And in truth he doesn’t need my help; you don’t know him as I do; he’s safe, he’s quite safe; mark my words, he’ll never be heard of again.”

5.5.oldText: The lawyer listened grimly; he didn’t like his friend’s feverish manner. “You seem quite sure of him,” he said. “And for your sake, I hope you’re right. If it came to a trial, your name might come up.”

5.6.oldText: “I’m quite sure of him,” Jekyll replied. “I have grounds for certainty that I can’t share with anyone. But there’s one thing you can advise me on. I have—I’ve received a letter, and I can’t decide whether I should show it to the police. I’d like to leave it in your hands, Utterson; you’d judge wisely, I’m sure; I have such great trust in you.”

5.7.oldText: “You’re afraid, I suppose, that it might lead to his capture?” asked the lawyer.

5.8.oldText: “No,” said the other. “I can’t say I care what becomes of Hyde; I’m quite done with him. I was thinking of my own reputation, which this hateful business has rather exposed.”

5.9.oldText: Utterson mulled this over for a while; he was surprised by his friend’s selfishness, and yet relieved by it. “Well,” he said at last, “let me see the letter.”

5.10.oldText: The letter was written in an odd, upright hand and signed “Edward Hyde”; and it stated, briefly enough, that the writer’s benefactor, Dr. Jekyll, whom he had for so long so unworthily repaid for a thousand kindnesses, need feel no alarm for his safety, since he had a means of escape on which he placed complete confidence. The lawyer liked this letter well enough; it cast a better light on the friendship than he had expected, and he blamed himself for some of his past suspicions.

5.12.oldText: “I burned it,” Jekyll replied, “before I thought about what I was doing. But it bore no postmark. The note was delivered by hand.”

5.13.oldText: “Shall I keep this and sleep on it?” asked Utterson.

5.14.oldText: “I want you to judge for me entirely,” was the reply. “I’ve lost confidence in myself.”

5.15.oldText: “Well, I’ll think it over,” the lawyer answered. “And now one more thing: was it Hyde who dictated the terms in your will about that disappearance?”

5.16.oldText: The doctor seemed seized by a fit of faintness; he shut his mouth tight and nodded.

5.17.oldText: “I knew it,” said Utterson. “He meant to murder you. You had a narrow escape.”

5.18.oldText: “I’ve had something far more to the point,” the doctor answered gravely: “I’ve had a lesson—oh God, Utterson, what a lesson I’ve had!” And he covered his face for a moment with his hands.

5.19.oldText: On his way out, the lawyer stopped and had a word or two with Poole. “By the way,” he said, “there was a letter delivered today: what did the messenger look like?” But Poole was certain that nothing had come except by post, “and only circulars at that,” he added.

5.20.oldText: This news sent the visitor off with his fears renewed. Clearly the letter had come by way of the laboratory door; quite possibly, in fact, it had been written in the study; and if that were so, it had to be judged differently, and handled with more caution. The newsboys, as he walked, were shouting themselves hoarse along the footpaths: “Special edition. Shocking murder of an M.P.” That was the funeral oration for one friend and client; and he couldn’t help feeling a certain dread that the good name of another might be dragged down into the whirlpool of the scandal. It was, at the very least, a delicate decision he had to make; and self-reliant as he was by habit, he began to wish for some advice. It wasn’t to be had directly; but perhaps, he thought, it might be fished for.

5.21.oldText: Presently he sat on one side of his own hearth, with Mr. Guest, his head clerk, on the other, and midway between them, at a carefully judged distance from the fire, a bottle of a particular old wine that had lain long unexposed to the sun in the depths of his cellar. The fog still lay sleeping on the wing above the drowned city, where the lamps glimmered like gems; and through the smother of these fallen clouds, the procession of the town’s life still rolled on through its great arteries with a sound like a mighty wind. But the room was cheerful with firelight. In the bottle the acids had long since mellowed; the deep colour had softened with age, the way the hue grows richer in stained glass windows; and the glow of hot autumn afternoons on hillside vineyards was ready to be set free and to scatter the fogs of London. Little by little the lawyer’s reserve melted. There was no man from whom he kept fewer secrets than Mr. Guest, and he wasn’t always sure he kept as many as he meant to. Guest had often been sent on business to the doctor’s house; he knew Poole; he could hardly have failed to hear of Mr. Hyde’s familiarity about the place; he might draw his own conclusions—so wasn’t it just as well, then, that he should see a letter that cleared up that mystery? And all the more since Guest, being a great student and critic of handwriting, would think the step natural and obliging. The clerk, besides, was a man of sound judgment; he could hardly read so strange a document without dropping some remark, and by that remark Mr. Utterson might shape his next move.

5.22.oldText: “This is a sad business about Sir Danvers,” he said.

5.23.oldText: “Yes, sir, indeed. It’s stirred up a great deal of public feeling,” Guest replied. “The man, of course, was mad.”

5.24.oldText: “I’d like to hear your thoughts on that,” Utterson replied. “I have a document here in his handwriting; it’s strictly between us, since I hardly know what to do about it; it’s an ugly business at best. But there it is—right up your street: a murderer’s autograph.”

5.25.oldText: Guest’s eyes lit up, and he sat down at once and studied it eagerly. “No, sir,” he said, “not mad; but it’s an odd hand.”

5.26.oldText: “And by all accounts a very odd writer,” the lawyer added.

5.27.oldText: Just then the servant came in with a note.

5.28.oldText: “Is that from Dr. Jekyll, sir?” the clerk asked. “I thought I knew the writing. Anything private, Mr. Utterson?”

5.29.oldText: “Just an invitation to dinner. Why? Do you want to see it?”

5.30.oldText: “One moment. I thank you, sir”; and the clerk laid the two sheets of paper side by side and carefully compared their contents. “Thank you, sir,” he said at last, handing both back. “It’s a very interesting autograph.”

5.31.oldText: There was a pause, during which Mr. Utterson struggled with himself. “Why did you compare them, Guest?” he asked suddenly.

5.32.oldText: “Well, sir,” the clerk replied, “there’s a rather striking resemblance; the two hands are identical in many points—only slanted differently.”

5.34.oldText: “It is, as you say, rather odd,” Guest replied.

5.35.oldText: “I wouldn’t mention this note, you know,” said Utterson.

5.37.oldText: But no sooner was Mr. Utterson alone that night than he locked the note away in his safe, where it stayed from that time forward. “What!” he thought. “Henry Jekyll forge a letter for a murderer!” And his blood ran cold in his veins.

7.0.oldText: It happened on a Sunday, when Mr. Utterson was out on his usual walk with Mr. Enfield, that their route took them once again through the by-street; and when they came to the door, both of them stopped to look at it.

7.1.oldText: “Well,” said Enfield, “that story is over, at least. We shall never see Mr. Hyde again.”

7.2.oldText: “I hope not,” said Utterson. “Did I ever tell you that I saw him once myself, and shared your feeling of disgust?”

7.3.oldText: “It was impossible to do one without the other,” Enfield replied. “And by the way, what a fool you must have thought me, not knowing that this was a back way into Dr. Jekyll’s! It was partly your own fault that I found it out, even when I did.”

7.4.oldText: “So you did find it out?” said Utterson. “Well, if that’s so, we may as well step into the court and take a look at the windows. To tell you the truth, I am uneasy about poor Jekyll; and even from outside, I feel as though a friend’s presence might do him good.”

7.5.oldText: The court was very cool and a little damp, and full of an early twilight, though high overhead the sky was still bright with sunset. The middle one of the three windows was half open; and sitting close beside it, taking the air with a look of boundless sadness, like some disconsolate prisoner, Utterson saw Dr. Jekyll.

7.6.oldText: “What! Jekyll! Jekyll!” he cried. “I trust you are better.”

7.7.oldText: “I am very low, Utterson,” the doctor replied drearily, “very low. It will not last long, thank God.”

7.8.oldText: “You stay indoors too much,” said the lawyer. “You ought to be out, getting your blood moving, like Mr. Enfield and me. (This is my cousin—Mr. Enfield—Dr. Jekyll.) Come now, get your hat and take a quick turn with us.”

7.9.oldText: “You are very kind,” the other sighed. “I should like to very much; but no, no, no, it is quite impossible; I dare not. But indeed, Utterson, I am very glad to see you; this is a real pleasure; I would ask you and Mr. Enfield up, but the place really is not fit.”

7.10.oldText: “Well, then,” said the lawyer good-naturedly, “the best thing we can do is stay down here and talk with you from where we are.”

7.11.oldText: “That is just what I was about to suggest,” the doctor answered with a smile. But the words were scarcely out before the smile was wiped from his face and replaced by such an expression of utter terror and despair that it froze the blood of the two men below. They caught only a glimpse of it, for the window was instantly pulled down; but that glimpse was enough, and they turned and left the court without a word. In silence, too, they made their way back through the by-street, and it was not until they had come into a nearby thoroughfare, where even on a Sunday there were still some signs of life, that Mr. Utterson finally turned and looked at his companion. Both were pale, and there was an answering horror in their eyes.

7.13.oldText: But Mr. Enfield only nodded very seriously and walked on again in silence.

8.0.oldText: Mr. Utterson was sitting by his fireside one evening after dinner, when he was surprised to receive a visit from Poole.

8.1.oldText: “Bless me, Poole, what brings you here?” he cried; and then, taking a second look at him, “What ails you?” he added. “Is the doctor ill?”

8.2.oldText: “Mr. Utterson,” said the man, “there is something wrong.”

8.3.oldText: “Take a seat, and here is a glass of wine for you,” said the lawyer. “Now, take your time, and tell me plainly what you want.”

8.4.oldText: “You know the doctor’s ways, sir,” replied Poole, “and how he shuts himself away. Well, he’s shut himself in the study again, and I don’t like it, sir—may I die if I like it. Mr. Utterson, sir, I’m afraid.”

8.5.oldText: “Now, my good man,” said the lawyer, “be explicit. What are you afraid of?”

8.6.oldText: “I’ve been afraid for about a week,” returned Poole, doggedly ignoring the question, “and I can bear it no more.”

8.7.oldText: The man’s look bore out his words; his manner had changed for the worse, and except for the moment he’d first announced his fear, he had not once met the lawyer’s eyes. Even now he sat with the glass of wine untouched on his knee, staring at a corner of the floor. “I can bear it no more,” he repeated.

8.8.oldText: “Come,” said the lawyer, “I see you have some good reason, Poole; I see there is something seriously wrong. Try to tell me what it is.”

8.9.oldText: “I think there’s been foul play,” said Poole hoarsely.

8.10.oldText: “Foul play!” cried the lawyer, badly frightened and, as a result, rather inclined to be irritated. “What foul play? What does the man mean?”

8.11.oldText: “I daren’t say, sir,” was the answer; “but will you come along with me and see for yourself?”

8.12.oldText: Mr. Utterson’s only answer was to rise and get his hat and overcoat; but he noticed, with wonder, how great the relief was on the butler’s face, and perhaps with no less wonder that the wine was still untouched when he set it down to follow.

8.13.oldText: It was a wild, cold March night, the kind you’d expect for the season: a pale moon lying on her back as if the wind had tipped her over, and thin, gauzy clouds racing past. The wind made talking difficult and stung colour into their faces. It seemed, besides, to have swept the streets unusually bare of passersby, for Mr. Utterson thought he had never seen that part of London so empty. He wished it were otherwise; never in his life had he felt so sharp a wish to see and touch his fellow human beings, for however hard he fought it, a crushing sense that something terrible was coming had settled over his mind. When they reached the square, it was full of wind and dust, and the thin trees in the garden lashed themselves against the railings. Poole, who had kept a pace or two ahead the whole way, now stopped in the middle of the pavement, and despite the biting cold, took off his hat and mopped his brow with a red handkerchief. But for all the haste of his coming, this was not the sweat of exertion he wiped away—it was the moisture of some choking anguish, for his face was white and his voice, when he spoke, harsh and broken.

8.14.oldText: “Well, sir,” he said, “here we are, and God grant there be nothing wrong.”

8.16.oldText: At that the servant knocked in a very cautious manner; the door was opened on the chain; and a voice asked from within, “Is that you, Poole?”

8.17.oldText: “It’s all right,” said Poole. “Open the door.”

8.18.oldText: The hall, when they entered it, was brightly lit; the fire was built up high; and around the hearth all the servants, men and women, stood huddled together like a flock of sheep. At the sight of Mr. Utterson, the housemaid broke into hysterical whimpering; and the cook, crying out, “Bless God! it’s Mr. Utterson,” ran forward as if to take him in her arms.

8.19.oldText: “What, what? Are you all here?” said the lawyer peevishly. “Very irregular, very unseemly; your master would be far from pleased.”

8.21.oldText: Blank silence followed, no one protesting; only the maid raised her voice and now wept loudly.

8.22.oldText: “Hold your tongue!” Poole snapped at her, with a fierceness that betrayed his own frayed nerves; and indeed, when the girl had so suddenly raised the note of her lament, they had all started and turned towards the inner door with faces full of dread. “Now,” the butler went on, turning to the knife-boy, “bring me a candle, and let’s get this over with at once.” Then he asked Mr. Utterson to follow him, and led the way to the back garden.

8.23.oldText: “Now, sir,” he said, “come as quietly as you can. I want you to hear, and I don’t want you to be heard. And listen, sir—if he should happen to ask you in, don’t go.”

8.24.oldText: Mr. Utterson’s nerves, at this unexpected turn, gave such a jolt that he nearly lost his balance; but he gathered his courage and followed the butler into the laboratory building, through the surgical theatre with its clutter of crates and bottles, to the foot of the stairs. There Poole motioned him to stand aside and listen, while he himself set down the candle, and, with a visible effort of will, climbed the steps and knocked, somewhat unsteadily, on the red baize of the study door.

8.25.oldText: “Mr. Utterson, sir, asking to see you,” he called; and even as he said it, he signalled urgently again for the lawyer to listen.

8.26.oldText: A voice answered from within: “Tell him I cannot see anyone,” it said, in a complaining tone.

8.27.oldText: “Thank you, sir,” said Poole, with something like triumph in his voice; and taking up his candle, he led Mr. Utterson back across the yard and into the great kitchen, where the fire was out and the beetles were leaping on the floor.

8.29.oldText: “It seems much changed,” replied the lawyer, very pale, but returning look for look.

8.30.oldText: “Changed? Well, yes, I think so,” said the butler. “Have I been twenty years in this man’s house, to be fooled about his voice? No, sir—my master’s been done away with; he was done away with eight days ago, when we heard him cry out in God’s name; and who’s in there instead of him, and why it stays there, is a thing that cries out to Heaven, Mr. Utterson!”

8.31.oldText: “That’s a very strange story, Poole; it’s a wild story, my man,” said Mr. Utterson, biting his finger. “Suppose it were as you suppose—suppose Dr. Jekyll had been, well, murdered—what could make the murderer stay? That doesn’t hold up; it doesn’t stand to reason.”

8.32.oldText: “Well, Mr. Utterson, you’re a hard man to satisfy, but I’ll manage it yet,” said Poole. “All this last week—you should know—him, or it, whatever it is that lives in that study, has been crying out night and day for some kind of medicine and can’t get it to suit him. It used to be his way—the master’s, I mean—to write his orders on a sheet of paper and throw it out onto the stairs. That’s all we’ve had this week: papers, a shut door, and even his meals left there to be smuggled in when no one was looking. Well, sir, every day—yes, and two or three times some days—there have been orders and complaints, and I’ve been sent flying to every wholesale chemist in town. Every time I brought the stuff back, there’d be another paper telling me to return it because it wasn’t pure, and another order to a different firm. This drug is wanted something terrible, sir, whatever it’s for.”

8.34.oldText: Poole felt in his pocket and handed over a crumpled note, which the lawyer, leaning nearer the candle, examined carefully. It read: “Dr. Jekyll presents his compliments to Messrs. Maw. He assures them that their last sample is impure and quite useless for his present purpose. In the year 18—, Dr. J. purchased a fairly large quantity from Messrs. M. He now asks them to search with the greatest care, and should any of the same quality remain, to send it to him at once. Expense is no consideration. The importance of this to Dr. J. can hardly be overstated.” So far the letter had run calmly enough, but here, with a sudden splutter of the pen, the writer’s feeling had broken loose. “For God’s sake,” he added, “find me some of the old.”

8.35.oldText: “This is a strange note,” said Mr. Utterson; and then sharply, “How is it you have it open?”

8.36.oldText: “The man at Maw’s was mighty angry, sir, and he threw it back at me like so much dirt,” returned Poole.

8.37.oldText: “This is unquestionably the doctor’s handwriting, don’t you think?” the lawyer went on.

8.38.oldText: “I thought it looked like it,” said the servant, rather sulkily; and then, in a different tone, “But what does handwriting matter?” he said. “I’ve seen him!”

8.40.oldText: “That’s it!” said Poole. “It happened like this. I came suddenly into the theatre from the garden. It seems he’d slipped out to look for this drug or whatever it is, because the study door was open, and there he was at the far end of the room, digging among the crates. He looked up when I came in, gave a kind of cry, and bolted upstairs into the study. I saw him for only a minute, but it made the hair stand up on my head like quills. Sir, if that was my master, why was he wearing a mask? If it was my master, why did he cry out like a rat and run from me? I’ve served him long enough. And then…” The man paused and passed his hand over his face.

8.41.oldText: “These are all very strange circumstances,” said Mr. Utterson, “but I think I’m beginning to see the light. Your master, Poole, is plainly in the grip of one of those diseases that both torture and disfigure the sufferer; that would explain, for all I know, the change in his voice; it would explain the mask and his avoidance of his friends; it would explain his eagerness to find this drug, by means of which the poor soul still hopes for eventual recovery—God grant he isn’t deceived! There’s my explanation; sad enough, Poole, yes, and dreadful to think about, but it’s plain and natural, it holds together, and it spares us from any excessive alarm.”

8.42.oldText: “Sir,” said the butler, turning a sort of blotchy pale, “that thing was not my master, and that’s the truth. My master”—here he looked around and began to whisper—“is a tall, well-built man, and that one was more of a dwarf.” Utterson tried to protest. “Oh, sir,” cried Poole, “do you think I don’t know my master after twenty years? Do you think I don’t know where his head comes to on the study door, where I saw him every morning of my life? No, sir, that thing in the mask was never Dr. Jekyll—God knows what it was, but it was never Dr. Jekyll; and in my heart I believe there’s been murder done.”

8.43.oldText: “Poole,” replied the lawyer, “if you say that, it becomes my duty to make certain. Much as I want to spare your master’s feelings, much as I am puzzled by this note which seems to prove he is still alive, I shall consider it my duty to break down that door.”

8.44.oldText: “Ah, Mr. Utterson, now you’re talking!” cried the butler.

8.45.oldText: “And now comes the second question,” Utterson went on: “Who is going to do it?”

8.46.oldText: “Why, you and me, sir,” was the fearless reply.

8.47.oldText: “Well said,” returned the lawyer; “and whatever comes of it, I shall make it my business to see that you don’t lose by it.”

8.48.oldText: “There’s an axe in the theatre,” Poole continued; “and you might take the kitchen poker for yourself.”

8.49.oldText: The lawyer took that crude but heavy tool in his hand and balanced it. “Do you know, Poole,” he said, looking up, “that you and I are about to put ourselves in some danger?”

8.50.oldText: “You may well say so, sir,” returned the butler.

8.51.oldText: “Then we’d better be honest with each other,” said the other. “We both think more than we’ve said; let’s speak plainly. This masked figure you saw—did you recognise it?”

8.52.oldText: “Well, sir, it moved so fast, and the creature was so hunched over, that I could hardly swear to it,” was the answer. “But if you mean, was it Mr. Hyde?—why, yes, I think it was! You see, it was much the same size, and it had the same quick, light way of moving; and besides, who else could have got in by the laboratory door? You haven’t forgotten, sir, that at the time of the murder he still had the key with him? But that’s not all. I don’t know, Mr. Utterson, whether you ever met this Mr. Hyde?”

8.53.oldText: “Yes,” said the lawyer, “I spoke with him once.”

8.54.oldText: “Then you must know as well as the rest of us that there was something odd about that gentleman—something that gave a man a turn—I don’t rightly know how to put it, sir, except this: that it made you feel cold and thin right down to your marrow.”

8.55.oldText: “I admit I felt something of what you describe,” said Mr. Utterson.

8.56.oldText: “Just so, sir,” returned Poole. “Well, when that masked thing jumped like a monkey out from among the chemicals and darted into the study, it went down my spine like ice. Oh, I know it’s not evidence, Mr. Utterson; I’m educated enough to know that; but a man has his feelings, and I give you my word on the Bible that it was Mr. Hyde!”

8.57.oldText: “Yes, yes,” said the lawyer. “My fears point the same way. I’m afraid evil was built into that connection from the start—evil was bound to come of it. Yes, truly, I believe you; I believe poor Harry has been killed; and I believe his murderer—for what purpose, God alone can tell—is still lurking in his victim’s room. Well, let vengeance be our watchword. Call Bradshaw.”

8.58.oldText: The footman came at the summons, very pale and nervous.

8.59.oldText: “Pull yourself together, Bradshaw,” said the lawyer. “This suspense, I know, is wearing on all of you; but we mean to put an end to it now. Poole and I are going to force our way into the study. If everything is all right, my shoulders are broad enough to bear the blame. But meanwhile, in case something really is wrong, or some wrongdoer tries to escape by the back, you and the boy must go round the corner with a pair of good sticks and take your post at the laboratory door. We give you ten minutes to get to your positions.”

8.60.oldText: As Bradshaw left, the lawyer checked his watch. “And now, Poole, let us get to ours,” he said, and, tucking the poker under his arm, led the way into the yard. Clouds had banked over the moon, and it was now quite dark. The wind, which only reached that deep well of a courtyard in gusts and draughts, tossed the candlelight back and forth about their steps, until they reached the shelter of the theatre, where they sat down in silence to wait. London hummed solemnly all around them, but nearer at hand the stillness was broken only by the sound of footsteps pacing back and forth across the study floor.

8.61.oldText: “So it goes, walking all day, sir,” Poole whispered; “yes, and most of the night too. Only when a new sample comes from the chemist is there any break in it. Ah, it’s a guilty conscience that’s such an enemy to rest! Ah, sir, there’s blood shed foully in every step of it! But listen again, come closer—put your whole heart into your ears, Mr. Utterson, and tell me, is that the doctor’s foot?”

8.62.oldText: The steps fell light and strange, with a certain sway to them, slow as they went; quite different from the heavy, creaking tread of Henry Jekyll. Utterson sighed. “Is there never anything else?” he asked.

8.64.oldText: “Weeping? How do you mean?” said the lawyer, feeling a sudden chill of horror.

8.65.oldText: “Weeping like a woman, or a lost soul,” said the butler. “I came away with that on my heart, so that I could have wept myself.”

8.66.oldText: But now the ten minutes were nearly up. Poole dug the axe out from under a stack of packing straw; the candle was set on the nearest table to light their attack; and they crept forward, holding their breath, to where that patient foot was still going up and down, up and down, in the stillness of the night.

8.67.oldText: “Jekyll,” Utterson cried in a loud voice, “I demand to see you.” He paused a moment, but no reply came. “I am warning you fairly, our suspicions are aroused, and I must and will see you,” he went on; “if not by fair means, then by foul—if not with your consent, then by force!”

8.69.oldText: “Ah, that’s not Jekyll’s voice—it’s Hyde’s!” cried Utterson. “Break down the door, Poole!”

8.70.oldText: Poole swung the axe over his shoulder; the blow shook the building, and the red baize door lurched against the lock and hinges. A dreadful shriek, like pure animal terror, rang out from the study. Up went the axe again, and again the panels cracked and the frame jumped; four times the blow fell, but the wood was tough and the fittings well made, and it was not until the fifth blow that the lock burst and the wreckage of the door fell inward onto the carpet.

8.71.oldText: The two men, shaken by the violence they had just done and by the silence that followed, drew back a little and looked in. There lay the study before their eyes in the quiet lamplight: a good fire glowing and crackling on the hearth, the kettle singing its thin note, a drawer or two open, papers neatly arranged on the desk, and, near the fire, things set out for tea—the quietest room, you would have said, and, but for the glass-fronted cabinets full of chemicals, the most ordinary room in London that night.

8.72.oldText: Right in the middle lay the body of a man, badly contorted and still twitching. They crept nearer on tiptoe, turned it onto its back, and saw the face of Edward Hyde. He was dressed in clothes far too large for him, clothes cut to the doctor’s size; the muscles of his face still moved as if with some trace of life, but life itself was quite gone; and by the crushed phial in his hand and the strong smell of kernels hanging in the air, Utterson knew he was looking at the body of a man who had killed himself.

8.73.oldText: “We have come too late,” he said sternly, “whether to save him or punish him. Hyde has gone to his reckoning; and all that’s left for us now is to find your master’s body.”

8.74.oldText: The greater part of the building was taken up by the theatre, which filled almost the whole ground floor and was lit from above, and by the study, which formed an upper floor at one end and looked out onto the courtyard. A corridor connected the theatre to the door on the side street, and the study was reached separately by a second flight of stairs. Besides these there were a few dark closets and a large cellar. They now searched all of it thoroughly. Each closet needed only a glance, since all were empty, and all, judging by the dust that fell from their doors, had stood unopened for a long time. The cellar, indeed, was filled with rickety old lumber, mostly left over from the surgeon who had owned the building before Jekyll; but even as they opened its door, a solid mat of cobweb that had sealed the entrance for years came falling down, telling them that further search there would be pointless. Nowhere was there any trace of Henry Jekyll, dead or alive.

8.76.oldText: “Or he may have fled,” said Utterson, and he turned to examine the door on the side street. It was locked, and lying nearby on the flagstones they found the key, already stained with rust.

8.77.oldText: “This does not look like it has been used,” observed the lawyer.

8.78.oldText: “Used!” echoed Poole. “Don’t you see, sir, it’s broken—as if someone had stamped on it?”

8.79.oldText: “Yes,” Utterson went on, “and the broken edges are rusty too.” The two men looked at each other, frightened. “This is beyond me, Poole,” said the lawyer. “Let us go back to the study.”

8.80.oldText: They climbed the stairs in silence, and, still glancing now and then in awe at the dead body, went on to examine the contents of the study more closely. On one table there were signs of chemical work: several measured heaps of some white salt laid out on glass dishes, as if for an experiment the unfortunate man had never got to finish.

8.81.oldText: “That’s the same drug I was always bringing him,” said Poole; and just as he spoke, the kettle boiled over with a startling noise.

8.82.oldText: This drew them to the fireside, where the easy chair stood cosily drawn up, and the tea things sat ready at the sitter’s elbow, sugar already in the cup. Several books stood on a shelf; one lay open beside the tea things, and Utterson was astonished to find it a copy of a devout work that Jekyll had more than once praised highly—annotated, in his own hand, with startling blasphemies.

8.83.oldText: Next, as they went on looking over the room, the searchers came to the tall standing mirror, into whose depths they looked with an involuntary sense of horror. But it was angled so as to show them nothing but the rosy glow playing across the ceiling, the fire sparkling over and over in the glazed fronts of the cabinets, and their own pale, frightened faces bending forward to look in.

8.84.oldText: “This mirror has seen some strange things, sir,” whispered Poole.

8.85.oldText: “And surely nothing stranger than itself,” echoed the lawyer in the same low voice. “For what did Jekyll”—he caught himself at the word with a start, then, overcoming the lapse—“what could Jekyll want with it?” he said.

8.86.oldText: “You may well say that!” said Poole.

8.87.oldText: Next they turned to the desk. Among the neat stack of papers, a large envelope lay on top, bearing, in the doctor’s hand, the name of Mr. Utterson. The lawyer broke the seal, and several enclosures fell to the floor. The first was a will, drawn up in the same eccentric terms as the one he had returned six months before—meant to serve as a testament in case of death and a deed of gift in case of disappearance—but in place of the name of Edward Hyde, the lawyer, with indescribable astonishment, read the name of Gabriel John Utterson. He looked at Poole, then back at the paper, and finally at the dead wrongdoer stretched on the carpet.

8.88.oldText: “My head is spinning,” he said. “He has been in possession of all this for days; he had no reason to like me; he must have raged to see himself replaced; and yet he has not destroyed this document.”

8.89.oldText: He picked up the next paper; it was a short note in the doctor’s hand, dated at the top. “Oh, Poole!” the lawyer cried, “he was alive and here today. He cannot have been got rid of in so short a time—he must still be alive, he must have fled! But then, why flee? And how? And in that case, can we really call this a suicide? Oh, we must be careful. I can see we may yet drag your master into some terrible catastrophe.”

8.91.oldText: “Because I am afraid to,” replied the lawyer solemnly. “God grant I have no reason to be!” And with that he lifted the paper to his eyes and read as follows:

8.92.oldText: “My dear Utterson,—By the time this reaches you, I will have disappeared, though under what circumstances I have no way of foreseeing; but my instinct, and everything about my nameless situation, tells me that the end is certain and must come soon. Go, then, and first read the account that Lanyon warned me he was to place in your hands; and if you care to hear more, turn to the confession of

8.95.oldText: “There was a third enclosure?” asked Utterson.

8.96.oldText: “Here, sir,” said Poole, and handed him a thick packet, sealed in several places.

8.97.oldText: The lawyer put it in his pocket. “I’d say nothing about this paper. If your master has fled or is dead, we may at least save his reputation. It is now ten; I must go home and read these documents in quiet, but I shall be back before midnight, when we shall send for the police.”

8.98.oldText: They went out, locking the door of the theatre behind them; and Utterson, once more leaving the servants gathered around the fire in the hall, trudged back to his office to read the two accounts that would now explain this mystery.

9.0.oldText: On the ninth of January, four days ago now, I received in the evening post a registered envelope addressed in the hand of my colleague and old school friend, Henry Jekyll. This surprised me a good deal, since we were by no means in the habit of writing to each other; I had seen the man, in fact dined with him, only the night before, and I could think of nothing in our dealings that would call for the formality of registration. What the letter said only deepened my surprise, for it read as follows:

9.2.oldText: “Dear Lanyon,—You are one of my oldest friends; and although we may have differed at times on scientific questions, I cannot remember, at least on my side, any break in our affection. There was never a day when, if you had said to me, ‘Jekyll, my life, my honour, my reason, depend upon you,’ I would not have sacrificed my left hand to help you. Lanyon, my life, my honour, my reason, are all at your mercy; if you fail me tonight, I am lost. You might suppose, after this preface, that I am going to ask you for something dishonourable. Judge for yourself.

9.3.oldText: “I want you to put off all other engagements for tonight—yes, even if you were summoned to the bedside of an emperor—take a cab, unless your own carriage should be actually at the door, and with this letter in hand for reference, drive straight to my house. Poole, my butler, has his orders; you will find him waiting for you with a locksmith. The door of my study is then to be forced, and you are to go in alone; open the glass-fronted cabinet (letter E) on the left, breaking the lock if it is shut, and draw out—with all its contents exactly as they stand—the fourth drawer from the top, or, which comes to the same thing, the third from the bottom. In my extreme distress of mind I have a morbid fear of giving you the wrong directions; but even if I am mistaken, you will know the right drawer by its contents: some powders, a phial, and a notebook. I beg you to carry this drawer back with you to Cavendish Square exactly as it stands.

9.4.oldText: “That is the first part of what I am asking; now for the second. If you set out at once on receiving this, you should be back long before midnight; but I will leave you that much margin, not only for fear of some obstacle that can neither be prevented nor foreseen, but because an hour when your servants are in bed is better suited to what will then remain to be done. At midnight, then, I ask you to be alone in your consulting room, to admit with your own hand into the house a man who will give my name at the door, and to place in his hands the drawer you will have brought back from my study. Then you will have played your part and earned my gratitude in full. Five minutes afterwards, if you insist on an explanation, you will understand that these arrangements, fantastic as they must appear, are of the utmost importance, and that neglecting even one of them might leave on your conscience my death or the wreck of my reason.

9.5.oldText: “Confident as I am that you will not make light of this appeal, my heart sinks and my hand trembles at the mere thought of such a possibility. Picture me at this hour, in a strange place, weighed down by a blackness of distress no imagination could exaggerate, and yet well aware that if you will only serve me punctually, my troubles will roll away like a story that is told. Serve me, my dear Lanyon, and save

9.8.oldText: “P.S.—I had already sealed this letter when a fresh terror struck upon my soul. It is possible the post office may fail me, and this letter not reach you until tomorrow morning. In that case, dear Lanyon, carry out my errand whenever it is most convenient for you in the course of the day, and once again expect my messenger at midnight. By then it may already be too late; and if that night passes without incident, you will know that you have seen the last of Henry Jekyll.”

9.9.oldText: On reading this letter, I felt sure my colleague had lost his mind; but until that was proved beyond all doubt, I felt bound to do as he asked. The less I understood of this jumble, the less I was in a position to judge how important it might be; and an appeal worded like this one could not be set aside without taking on a grave responsibility. So I rose from the table, got into a hansom, and drove straight to Jekyll’s house. The butler was expecting my arrival; he had received, by the same post as mine, a registered letter of instructions, and had already sent for a locksmith and a carpenter. The tradesmen arrived while we were still talking, and we all moved together to old Dr. Denman’s surgical theatre, from which—as you are doubtless aware—Jekyll’s private study is most conveniently entered. The door was very strong, the lock excellent; the carpenter admitted he would have great trouble and would have to do much damage if force were used, and the locksmith was near despair. But this last was a capable fellow, and after two hours’ work the door stood open. The cabinet marked E was unlocked; I took out the drawer, had it packed with straw and tied up in a sheet, and returned with it to Cavendish Square.

9.10.oldText: There I proceeded to examine its contents. The powders were made up neatly enough, but not with a dispensing chemist’s precision, so it was plain they were of Jekyll’s own manufacture; and when I opened one of the wrappers I found what seemed to me a simple crystalline salt, white in colour. The phial, to which I turned next, might have been about half full of a blood-red liquid, highly pungent to the smell and seeming to contain phosphorus along with some volatile ether. At the other ingredients I could make no guess. The notebook was an ordinary exercise book and contained little but a series of dates. These covered a period of many years, but I noticed the entries stopped nearly a year ago, quite abruptly. Here and there a brief remark was added to a date, usually no more than a single word: “double,” occurring perhaps six times in a total of several hundred entries; and once, very early in the list, followed by several exclamation marks, “total failure!!!” All this, though it sharpened my curiosity, told me little that was definite. Here were a phial of some salt and the record of a series of experiments that had led, like too many of Jekyll’s investigations, to nothing of any practical use. How could the presence of these things in my house affect either the honour, the sanity, or the life of my flighty colleague? If his messenger could go to one place, why could he not go to another? And even granting some obstacle, why should this gentleman be received by me in secret? The more I reflected, the more convinced I grew that I was dealing with a case of brain disease; and though I sent my servants off to bed, I loaded an old revolver, so that I might be found in some posture of self-defence.

9.11.oldText: Twelve o’clock had scarcely finished sounding over London when the knocker sounded, very gently, on the door. I went myself at the summons, and found a small man crouching against the pillars of the portico.

9.13.oldText: He told me “yes” by a constrained gesture; and when I had asked him in, he did not obey without first casting a searching glance back into the darkness of the square. A policeman was not far off, advancing with his bull’s-eye open, and at the sight of him, I thought my visitor started and hurried his steps.

9.14.oldText: These details struck me, I confess, unpleasantly; and as I followed him into the bright light of the consulting room, I kept my hand ready on my weapon. Here, at last, I had a chance of seeing him clearly. I had never set eyes on him before, that much was certain. He was small, as I have said; and I was struck, besides, by the shocking expression of his face, by his remarkable combination of great muscular energy and great apparent frailty of constitution—and, last but not least, by the odd, personal disturbance his nearness caused in me. This bore some resemblance to the onset of a chill, and came with a marked drop in my pulse. At the time I set it down to some private, idiosyncratic distaste of my own, and merely wondered at how sharp the symptoms were; but I have since come to believe the cause lies far deeper in the nature of man, and turns on some nobler hinge than mere hatred.

9.15.oldText: This person—who had, from the very first moment of his entrance, stirred in me what I can only describe as a repelled curiosity—was dressed in a fashion that would have made an ordinary man ridiculous; his clothes, that is to say, though of rich and sober fabric, were enormously too large for him in every measurement—the trousers hanging on his legs and rolled up to keep them off the ground, the waist of the coat below his hips, and the collar sprawling wide upon his shoulders. Strange to relate, this absurd getup was far from moving me to laughter. Rather, since there was something abnormal and misbegotten in the very essence of the creature now facing me—something arresting, startling, and revolting—this further oddity seemed only to fit with and reinforce it; so that to my interest in the man’s nature and character was added a curiosity as to his origin, his life, his fortune, and his standing in the world.

9.16.oldText: These observations, though they have taken so much space to set down, were the work of only a few seconds. My visitor was, in fact, on fire with a sombre excitement.

9.17.oldText: “Have you got it?” he cried. “Have you got it?” And so keen was his impatience that he even laid his hand on my arm and tried to shake me.

9.18.oldText: I pushed him back, aware at his touch of a certain icy pang through my blood. “Come, sir,” I said. “You forget that I have not yet had the pleasure of your acquaintance. Be seated, if you please.” And I showed him an example, taking my own usual seat myself, doing as fair an imitation of my ordinary manner with a patient as the lateness of the hour, the nature of my preoccupations, and the horror I had of my visitor would allow me to manage.

9.19.oldText: “I beg your pardon, Dr. Lanyon,” he replied civilly enough. “What you say is very fair; my impatience has got the better of my manners. I come here at the request of your colleague, Dr. Henry Jekyll, on a matter of some importance, and I understood…” He paused and put his hand to his throat, and I could see, despite his composed manner, that he was struggling against the onset of hysteria—“I understood, a drawer…”

9.20.oldText: But here I took pity on my visitor’s suspense, and perhaps a little on my own growing curiosity.

9.22.oldText: He sprang towards it, then paused, and pressed his hand to his heart; I could hear his teeth grinding with the convulsive working of his jaw, and his face was so ghastly that I grew alarmed both for his life and his reason.

9.24.oldText: He turned a dreadful smile on me, and, as if with the resolve of despair, tore away the sheet. At the sight of what lay inside, he let out one loud sob of such immense relief that I sat there petrified. And the next moment, in a voice already fairly well under control, “Have you a graduated glass?” he asked.

9.25.oldText: I rose from my place with some effort and gave him what he asked for.

9.26.oldText: He thanked me with a smiling nod, measured out a few minims of the red tincture, and added one of the powders. The mixture, which was at first a reddish hue, began, as the crystals dissolved, to brighten in colour, to fizz audibly, and to throw off small clouds of vapour. Suddenly, at that same moment, the fizzing stopped and the compound changed to a dark purple, which then faded, more slowly, to a watery green. My visitor, who had watched these changes with a sharp eye, smiled, set the glass down on the table, and then turned and looked at me with an air of scrutiny.

9.27.oldText: “And now,” he said, “to settle what remains. Will you be wise? Will you be guided? Will you let me take this glass in my hand and go out of your house without further talk? Or has the greed of curiosity too much command of you? Think before you answer, for it shall be as you decide. Decide one way, and you shall be left exactly as you were, neither richer nor wiser, unless the sense of having served a man in mortal distress may be counted as a kind of riches of the soul. Or, if you would rather choose otherwise, a new province of knowledge and new avenues to fame and power shall be laid open to you, here, in this room, upon the instant; and your sight shall be blasted by a marvel to stagger the disbelief of Satan himself.”

9.28.oldText: “Sir,” I said, affecting a coolness I was far from truly feeling, “you speak in riddles, and you will perhaps not be surprised that I hear you with no very strong impression of belief. But I have gone too far along this road of inexplicable services to stop now before I see the end of it.”

9.29.oldText: “It is well,” my visitor replied. “Lanyon, remember your vows: what follows is under the seal of our profession. And now, you who have so long been bound to the most narrow and material views, you who have denied the power of transcendental medicine, you who have mocked your betters—behold!”

9.30.oldText: He put the glass to his lips and drank it down in one gulp. A cry followed; he reeled, staggered, clutched at the table and held on, staring with bloodshot eyes, gasping with open mouth; and as I watched, a change seemed to come over him—he appeared to swell—his face suddenly turned black and his features seemed to melt and shift—and the next moment I had sprung to my feet and leapt back against the wall, my arms raised to shield me from that marvel, my mind sinking into terror.

9.31.oldText: “Oh God!” I screamed, and “Oh God!” again and again; for there before my eyes—pale and shaken, half fainting, groping before him with his hands like a man risen from the dead—there stood Henry Jekyll!

9.32.oldText: What he told me in the hour that followed, I cannot bring my mind to set down on paper. I saw what I saw, I heard what I heard, and my soul sickened at it; and yet now, when that sight has faded from my eyes, I ask myself whether I believe it, and I cannot answer. My life is shaken to its roots; sleep has left me; the deadliest terror sits by me at all hours of the day and night; and I feel that my days are numbered, and that I must die; and yet I shall die unconvinced. As for the moral corruption that man unveiled to me, even with tears of penitence, I cannot, even in memory, dwell on it without a start of horror. I will say but one thing, Utterson, and that—if you can bring your mind to believe it—will be more than enough.
